name: Zerodha
summary: Zerodha is the Indian discount broker behind Kite, Coin, Console and the Varsity learning modules. It says it hires people with good skills who learn quickly and work well in a team, and values that over years of experience. Candidates commonly describe a less standardised process than at many firms, built around conversations about their own work, and the steps vary by team.
rounds: Application through Zerodha's careers site, often with links to your work: projects, code or writing
A screening conversation about your background and why Zerodha
One or more technical or functional discussions, often going deep into one project you built
A practical task or work sample for some roles
A final conversation on fit, expectations and long-term intent, often with a senior team member
looks_for: Good skills and the ability to learn quickly, valued over years of experience
Being a team player who keeps learning and does what needs doing (Zerodha calls this non-negotiable)
Being in it for the long haul, with expectations set right from the start
Proof of real work: projects, code or writing you can show and explain
Simple, lean solutions over elaborate ones
Care for investors' interests and clear, honest communication

questions.text: Tell me about a project you built on your own time. Why did you build it, and what did you learn?
covers: The problem that made you start it, ideally your own or a friend's
Key choices you made and the ones you'd now undo
Who used it, what broke, and what it taught you

questions.text: Tell me about a time you had to learn a new tool or domain quickly to get something working.
covers: Why it was needed and how little time you had
How you learned: docs, source code, small experiments, people you asked
What you shipped and how well you understand it now

questions.text: Describe a time you simplified a system or process instead of adding to it.
covers: What was complicated and what it cost: time, money, errors
What you removed or replaced, and why that was safe
The result after the change, with a number if you have one

questions.text: Tell me about a time you did work outside your job description because it needed doing.
covers: The gap you noticed and why nobody owned it
What you did and how you kept your own work on track
What changed for the team or customers

questions.text: Tell me about a mistake you made that affected other people. How did you handle it?
covers: The mistake, owned plainly and early in the answer
Who you told, how quickly, and how you limited the damage
The habit or check you added so it doesn't happen again

questions.text: At market open, orders and logins arrive in a burst within seconds. How would you design a trading backend to stay stable through it?
covers: Separating the critical order path from everything else, such as reports and charts
Queues, back-pressure and rate limits so a burst doesn't topple the system
Load testing against the opening burst, and what you'd degrade first if needed

questions.text: How would you stream live prices for thousands of instruments to a very large number of users at once? Talk me through your approach.
covers: Persistent connections (such as WebSockets) and sending only subscribed instruments
Compact message formats and throttling updates per client
Fan-out with pub/sub, and what happens when a client is slow or reconnects

questions.text: A customer says an order showed as placed in the app but never reached the exchange. How would you investigate?
covers: Tracing the order by its ID and timestamps through each system it passed
Checking for a gap: a timeout, a rejected request, a status shown too early
Keeping the customer informed, and fixing the root cause, not just this order

questions.text: Explain the difference between a stock and a mutual fund, and between delivery and intraday trades, to a first-time investor.
covers: A stock is a share in one company; a fund pools money across many holdings
Delivery means holding shares in your demat account; intraday closes the same day
The extra risk of intraday trading, said plainly and without jargon

questions.text: When would you choose a simple self-hosted tool over a managed cloud service? Give an example from your work.
covers: Cost, control, data ownership and how well the team can run it
The operational work self-hosting adds: upgrades, backups, monitoring
A real example and whether you'd make the same choice again

questions.text: How would you write an explainer that helps a beginner understand what a futures contract is, and its risks?
covers: Starting from an everyday example before any jargon
Leverage and margin explained with a simple worked example
Being honest about losses and who the product isn't suited for

questions.text: A new regulatory rule means a feature must change within weeks. How would you plan the work and tell customers?
covers: Reading the rule closely and agreeing what exactly must change
A plan with a buffer, testing, and a fallback if the date is at risk
Telling customers early, in plain words, what changes for them

questions.text: Why Zerodha, and what do you see yourself working on here over the long term?
covers: A reason tied to its products or way of working, not just the brand
What you'd like to own over several years
Expectations you're setting honestly: learning, responsibility, pace

questions.text: Zerodha says it has no conventional titles or career ladder. How do you think about growth in a place like that?
covers: Growth as more responsibility and harder problems, not a new title
How you'd measure your own progress
An example of growing in a role without a promotion

questions.text: Which part of Kite, Coin, Console or Varsity have you used, and what would you improve?
covers: Specific use: what you did with it and when
One concrete improvement and who it would help
What you'd leave out to keep the product simple

tips: Bring proof of work: a repository, a deployed project, a write-up or an article you can walk through in detail.
Use Kite, Coin and Console before the interview, and read a few Varsity modules if you're applying for a non-tech role.
Expect depth over breadth: be ready to explain every decision in one project, including what you'd remove.
Zerodha's tech blog writes openly about how it builds; reading a few posts gives you good questions to ask.
Be clear about why you want to stay long term; Zerodha says it hires people who are in it for the long haul.

sources.title: On Growth, Hiring, and Thinking Long Term (Zerodha Z-Connect)
